channel.title: NeuroBrief · 静息态与自然刺激
channel.description: 静息态，以及电影、故事、自然语音与语篇理解中的脑活动

item.title: Spontaneously emerging patterns show category-biased similarity to task-evoked visual patterns beyond human visual cortex.
item.description:
NeuroImage
In the absence of any task, spontaneous brain activity exhibits patterns that resemble those evoked by natural stimuli and behaviors. This raises the possibility that resting-state activity patterns may relate to maintenance and consolidation of behaviorally relevant information states. Using functional MRI (fMRI) data from 100 healthy adults in the Human Connectome Project, we investigated whether neural signals evoked by specific visual stimuli (body parts, faces, places, tools) show similarity to resting-state activity across non-canonical visual areas, i.e., motor and association cortices. Participants underwent a working memory task and resting-state scanning. We analyzed multivoxel pattern similarity between task-evoked activations and spontaneous activity in bilateral hand motor regions and attention-related networks. Spatial correlations between task-evoked multivoxel patterns for each visual category and frame-by-frame resting-state signals were computed, with the upper 90% distribution percentile (U90) as a similarity metric. We found that resting-state patterns in the left hemisphere hand motor region showed significantly higher similarity to tool-evoked patterns than place-evoked patterns, consistent with the interpretation that tools recruit motor affordances and hand‑object associations in motor cortex. In the bilateral dorsal attention network, resting-task similarity for non-face evoked patterns significantly exceeded that for faces. Moreover, effects localized to posterior dorsal attention network, aligning with the dorsal visual pathway's role in spatial-action coding of behaviorally relevant objects. These results suggest that resting-state activity in non-visual cortices shows category-biased similarity to task-evoked visual patterns, consistent with the view that spontaneous neural dynamics preferentially reactivate ecologically salient stimuli.

item.title: Evaluation of Brain Activity in Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder Using Standardized Low Resolution Electromagnetic Tomographic Analyses (sLORETA).
item.description:
Clinical EEG and neuroscience
This study evaluated Default Mode Network (DMN) brain activity in females with Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD)/Dysphoric PMS and asymptomatic controls using archival quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG) and standardized low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (sLORETA) data. Eyes-closed resting-state EEG analyses were examined across follicular and luteal menstrual cycle phases. The analytic sample included 157 participants: PMDD/Dysphoric PMS (n = 87) and asymptomatic controls (n = 70). Nonparametric Wilcoxon Signed Rank Tests were used for follicular-to-luteal within-group comparisons, and Mood's Median Test was used for luteal-phase between-group analyses. Asymptomatic controls showed significant follicular-to-luteal mean-Z changes in cingulate gyrus delta, cingulate gyrus theta, and insula theta. PMDD/Dysphoric PMS participants showed a significant percentage-of-aberrant-voxels change in angular gyrus beta2. During the luteal phase, PMDD/Dysphoric PMS participants showed significantly higher subcallosal-gyrus beta2 mean-Z activity than asymptomatic controls. Luteal subcallosal-gyrus beta2 abnormal-voxel values were descriptively higher in PMDD/Dysphoric PMS participants (19.43%) than in asymptomatic controls (4.13%); however, this voxel-percentage comparison is reported descriptively because luteal-phase between-group percentage-of-voxels analyses did not reach the study threshold for statistical significance. These findings support further investigation of DMN-linked neural activity, subcallosal-gyrus beta2 activity, and phase-related network adaptability in PMDD.

item.title: From sensorimotor to transmodal cortex: sleep quality aligns brain entropy with the cortical functional gradient.
item.description:
Sleep
STUDY OBJECTIVES: Sleep is fundamental to brain health, yet the mechanisms by which habitual sleep quality shapes large-scale neural dynamics during wakefulness remain unclear. This work aims at determining whether habitual sleep quality is associated with systematic alterations in regional and cross-regional temporal complexity of spontaneous neural activity. METHODS: Regional brain entropy (BEN) and cross-regional brain entropy were estimated from resting-state fMRI data of the UK Biobank, with replication in the Human Connectome Project and in a randomized total sleep deprivation experiment. Temporal complexity of spontaneous neural activity was correlated to self-reported habitual sleep quality and sleep amount in observational cohorts and experimental total sleep deprivation in the laboratory study. RESULTS: Better sleep quality was associated with increased BEN in sensory and sensorimotor cortices and decreased BEN in frontoparietal control regions. High-quality sleep enhanced differentiation of temporal complexity among sensory networks while strengthening coordination within higher-order control systems. In the independent Human Connectome Project cohort, sleep amount predicted increased BEN in visual and somatomotor regions. Moreover, the strength of the association between sleep measures and BEN was strongly and negatively correlated with the major cortical functional gradient. Exploratory results suggest convergent effects following total sleep deprivation. Habitual sleep quality is associated with systematic reconfiguration of the brain's temporal complexity architecture at both regional and network levels. CONCLUSION: These findings position sleep as a fundamental determinant of the brain's dynamic operating regime and identify temporal complexity as a mechanistically informative neural signature linking sleep health to cognitive function and neuropsychiatric vulnerability.

item.title: Neural Connectome Mapping of Chronotype in Young Adults: Associations with Neurotransmitter Profiles and Longitudinal Self-Control.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Chronotype is associated with self-regulation, but its functional connectivity correlates, neurotransmitter correspondence, and longitudinal associations with self-control remain unclear. We applied connectome-based predictive modeling (CPM) in a longitudinal cohort to identify resting-state connectivity features associated with chronotype. Cross-validated predictions showed a small correlation with reduced Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (rMEQ) scores in the discovery set (n = 816, r = 0.118, pperm = 0.007). A similar association was observed in validation set 1, a baseline hold-out sample from the same cohort (n = 681, r = 0.125, pperm < 0.001). Longitudinal evaluation used validation set 2, comprising two-year follow-up data from a subset of participants in validation set 1 (n = 594, r = 0.134, pperm < 0.001), providing a within-cohort assessment of whether the association was stable over time. Node-importance maps showed spatial correspondence with neurotransmitter maps. Both connectivity sets shared GABA-A and VAChT associations, with relatively receptor-weighted and transporter-weighted profiles in the positive and negative sets, respectively. In participants with complete two-wave data (n = 563), cross-lagged panel models indicated that baseline self-control was prospectively associated with higher positive-set strength (β = 0.256, p < 0.001) and lower negative-set strength (β = -0.228, p < 0.001); reverse paths were not significant. These findings provide evidence for chronotype-related functional connectivity features and their associations with neurotransmitter distributions and self-control in young adults. The validation and longitudinal evidence is limited to a single-site cohort, and cross-cohort generalizability remains to be established.

item.title: Static and dynamic intrinsic brain activity in eyes-closed and eyes-open resting-state conditions.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data are typically acquired under eyes-closed (EC) or eyes-open (EO) conditions, which are thought to reflect interoceptive and exteroceptive brain states. However, evidence for condition-dependent differences has largely relied on static analyses that provide limited information about temporal variability. Here, we investigated eye-state modulation of intrinsic brain activity by integrating multimetric static and dynamic analyses across multiple spatial scales. Static measures, including the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), fractional ALFF (fALFF), regional homogeneity (ReHo), and degree centrality (DC), were estimated to characterize low-frequency amplitude, relative spectral contribution, local synchronization, and network centrality. A sliding-window approach was used to calculate ALFF, fALFF, ReHo, and DC within successive windows, and their variability across windows was quantified. Static analyses revealed spatial differences between EC and EO across visual, sensorimotor, temporal, prefrontal, parietal, and subcortical regions. A particularly consistent finding across the static metrics was greater middle occipital gyrus involvement during EO. However, fALFF also showed an EC-related increase in the left calcarine cortex, indicating regionally heterogeneous effects within the occipital cortex. Dynamic analyses showed greater variability during EC in selected posterior visual regions, most consistently for dALFF and dReHo variability, whereas dfALFF and dDC variability were more sensitive to window length, mean adjustment, and spatial standardization. These findings demonstrate that eye state modulates intrinsic brain function through coordinated changes in both whole-scan measures and temporal variability across multiple spatial scales, highlighting the importance of jointly considering static and dynamic properties when investigating the neural organization of resting-state activity.

item.title: The unfolding symphony: unraveling brain dynamics via data-driven multi-scale functional connectivity in task-state fMRI.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Task-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) can characterize both regional responses and changes in statistical dependence among distributed brain systems. This narrative review examines dynamic and multiscale connectivity within a broader framework that distinguishes task-modulated functional connectivity, trial-wise covariation, effective connectivity, and data-driven state analysis. Sliding-window correlation, hidden Markov models, and co-activation patterns are compared by their data representations, temporal assumptions, and computational procedures; graph representations can be combined with each of these strategies. We discuss supervised recurrent, transformer, and graph models alongside unsupervised state discovery, self-supervised representation learning, and emerging brain foundation models. Explainability requires evaluation of model attributions, including graph masks and perturbation-based analyses, rather than anatomical plausibility alone. The spatial framework includes whole-brain networks, subnetworks, atlas-defined regions of interest, and voxel- or layer-level measurements. Proposed links across these levels remain hypotheses: faster sampling of the blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) signal does not directly resolve millisecond neural interactions, and resting-state or animal findings do not establish the corresponding mechanism during human tasks. Shared task-evoked responses, hemodynamic variability, motion, and analytical choices can all alter apparent connectivity. Progress therefore depends on matching the estimator to the scientific question, comparing against activation and static-connectivity baselines, and validating results across participants, sessions, and acquisition settings.

item.title: Functional brain connectivity in patients with anorexia nervosa before and after short-term weight restoration.
item.description:
Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines
BACKGROUND: Resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) studies have consistently identified widespread alterations in the brain's functional network architecture in anorexia nervosa (AN), but it remains unclear whether they are reversible with weight restoration. Furthermore, it is not clear whether there are associations between RSFC and neuroendocrine changes, such as leptin suppression in the underweight state of AN and its increase during short-term weight restoration. METHODS: We first analyzed RSFC data cross-sectionally in young female patients with AN (n = 117) and healthy control participants (n = 117) using network-based statistic (NBS) and graph theory metrics and subsequently explored relationships with plasma leptin as a marker of undernutrition. A subset of patients (n = 73) was reassessed longitudinally after short-term weight restoration [mean body mass index (BMI) increase: 28.0%] to test for changes in identified alterations. RESULTS: NBS revealed increased RSFC in cingulo-occipito-cerebellar circuitry in underweight patients with AN (p = .0018), which decreased over the inpatient weight restoration interval (p < .001). This change correlated negatively with plasma leptin concentrations (p = .042), and plasma leptin appeared to partially mediate the association between BMI increase and RSFC decrease (p = .039), suggesting a possible region-specific modulatory effect. Underweight patients with AN also showed higher characteristic path length (p = .035), indicating reduced integration between brain regions, and higher assortativity (p = .013), indicating stronger coupling among similarly connected regions. Longitudinally, characteristic path length decreased during weight restoration (p = .004), whereas findings for assortativity were suggestive of no change. CONCLUSIONS: The results provide novel longitudinal evidence that functional connectome alterations in AN partially normalize during short-term weight restoration. Speculatively, taking previous results in long-term recovered individuals into consideration, higher assortativity might reflect potential vulnerability for AN. Our finding of a tentative association between the normalization of plasma leptin concentrations and RSFC suggests the possibility that leptin may modulate changes in specific patterns of functional connectivity, offering a potential neurobiological target for novel pharmacotherapies.

item.title: Glycemic control is differentially related to spontaneous cortical activity in patients on the Alzheimer's disease spectrum.
item.description:
GeroScience
Diabetes is a major risk factor for developing cognitive impairment and studies have shown that poor glycemic control can increase this risk, but the neural mechanisms are poorly understood. Many studies have linked altered spontaneous cortical activity during the resting-state to Alzheimer's disease and other neurological conditions associated with cognitive impairment. Herein, we examine whether the strength of spontaneous activity during the resting-state is differentially related to glycemic control in 37 biomarker-positive participants on the Alzheimer's disease spectrum (ADS) and 43 cognitively normal aging adults. All participants completed resting-state magnetoencephalography (MEG), a blood draw to derive their level of glycemic control (i.e., A1C), and comprehensive neuropsychological assessment. Spontaneous activity was imaged in each of the canonical frequency bands (e.g., alpha) and probed for group differences in the relationship between neural activity and glycemic control. We found significant interactions between A1C and disease status (ADS vs. control) in the delta and alpha bands (p < 0.001). Specifically, delta power decreased with increasing A1C in the ADS group across a broad area of frontotemporal and inferior parietal cortices, while spontaneous alpha decreased with higher A1C in the control group across inferior frontal and temporal cortex. Importantly, delta activity in the superior frontal cortices mediated the effect of A1C on attention performance in the ADS group. In sum, these data suggest that the impact of glycemic dysregulation on spontaneous cortical activity may differ in those on the ADS compared with cognitively normal controls and that spontaneous delta may be critical for attention function.

item.title: Altered EEG-derived co-fluctuation structure in disorders of consciousness.
item.description:
Cognitive neurodynamics
EEG-derived functional connectivity (FC) enables high-temporal-resolution probing of neural mechanisms underlying disorders of consciousness (DOC). Unlike stationary conventional FC, dynamic FC (dFC) captures fast transient neural coupling. Recent fMRI studies introduced a co‑fluctuation framework to track moment‑to‑moment connectivity change, yet whether such co-fluctuation features can quantify consciousness status remains elusive. Here, we adapt this established co-fluctuation paradigm to resting-state EEG to characterize the temporal architectures of EEG-derived FC across varying conscious states. We decomposed the co-fluctuation time series into high-amplitude frames (HAF) and low-amplitude frames (LAF), comparing their dynamics between real brain data and null models. We then analyzed co-fluctuation activities across consciousness levels at both global and local spatial scales, examining spatial variability in these patterns. By integrating HAF and LAF parameters, we evaluated their diagnostic potential for distinguishing DOC states. Results revealed reduced stability of co-fluctuations with loss of consciousness, accompanied by a shift toward random system dynamics. DOC patients exhibited reduced spatial and temporal heterogeneity in co-fluctuation activities compared to healthy controls. Both high- and low-amplitude patterns provided useful metrics for detecting consciousness levels. These findings offer novel insights into the dynamic organization of brain networks in DOC, emphasizing the significance of co-fluctuation dynamics in characterizing brain states and suggesting potential biomarkers for assessing consciousness levels. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11571-026-10580-7.

item.title: Greater Stress Response Network (SRN) Connectivity is Associated with Higher Worry in Men and Women Especially in Later Life
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Late-life anxiety is common and disabling, with pathological worry as a core feature. The Stress Response Network (SRN: amygdala, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, paraventricular nucleus), which modulates threat and stress reactivity, and its interaction with the Executive Control Network (ECN), anchored by the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which supports emotional regulation via top-down cognitive control, may underlie individual differences in worry severity. We hypothesize higher SRN connectivity to be associated with greater worry severity and that this relationship may be moderated positively by older age, and female sex. Methods: We recruited older adults with varying worry. Resting-state fMRI was used to compute SRN connectivity and SRN-ECN connectivity. Regression models tested associations between connectivity and worry (PSWQ), anxiety (HARS), and rumination (RSQ), adjusting for age, sex, race, and education. Exploratory models examined age and sex moderation and associations with emotion regulation/suppression and cognitive function. Results: Among 131 participants who were ≥ 50 years old, with varying levels of worry severity, SRN connectivity was significantly associated with greater worry severity (B=23.51 (SE = 12.12), p<0.05), whereas SRN-ECN connectivity was not. SRN connectivity was lower with greater age (B=-0.003 (SE=0.001), p=0.04), yet older individuals reported greater worry than younger with comparable connectivity. Greater language domain cognitive function was associated with lower SRN connectivity but higher SRN-ECN connectivity, while greater overall cognitive function was associated with lower SRN-ECN connectivity. Women reported lower use of daily expressive suppression and higher performance across cognitive measures than men. Higher daily use of expressive suppression was not significantly associated with either connectivity measure. Discussion: SRN connectivity, rather than SRN-ECN connectivity, may serve as the primary neural correlate of worry, shaped by age and cognitive function.

item.title: Spatially localized fMRI metrics as predictive and highly distinct state-independent fingerprints.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Precision medicine and the investigation of brain-behavior associations require biomarkers that are stable (low intraindividual variability) and unique (high-interindividual variability) at the same time, hence calling them "fingerprints". The functional connectome (FC) has good "fingerprint properties", as individuals can be accurately identified in a database based on their FC. Importantly, research has shown lower intraindividual variability of more localized measures of brain function, such as regional homogeneity (ReHo) and (fractional) amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations ((f)ALFF), compared with the FC. Additionally, the predictiveness of behavior using the FC is modest at best. Here, with fMRI data from two publicly available datasets, we demonstrate that individuals can be identified with near-perfect accuracies using local functional fingerprints, especially the regional homogeneity (ReHo) fingerprint. Further analyses reveal that the dorsal attention network contributes most to the individual "uniqueness" of the ReHo fingerprint. Moreover, using a machine learning setup, we find that intraindividual variability of the ReHo fingerprint across sessions shows predictive signal for individual-level intelligence, albeit with model performance dependent on the condition. Last, using two other publicly available datasets, clinical applicability is demonstrated with high fingerprint accuracies and a significant correlation between fingerprint stability and intelligence in individuals with schizophrenia. Altogether, our findings suggest that the ReHo fingerprint is a good candidate for further exploration of applicability in precision medicine.

item.title: Short-Video Experience and Brain-State Dynamics During the Processing of Rapidly Changing Video Information in Youth.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Background Short-video platforms frequently expose youth to rapidly changing video information. Processing such inputs requires large-scale brain networks to reorganize with the ongoing context. However, little is known about these dynamics or their association with prior short-video viewing experience. Methods A total of 108 youth aged 8-18 years completed resting-state and naturalistic movie-viewing fMRI scans. The movie comprised rapidly changing and relatively continuous segments. Hidden Markov models were applied to 17 cortical networks to identify recurrent brain states, and a joint rest-task analysis examined the context specificity of the main finding. Results Eight task-related brain states were identified. Five differed in fractional occupancy (FO) between conditions, and global switching was slightly higher during rapidly changing segments. State 7 was the only state showing an interaction with short-video viewing experience. Its FO was higher during relatively continuous than rapidly changing segments among participants reporting no prior Douyin use, whereas the condition difference was not significant among those reporting prior Douyin use. Visit frequency analyses showed a similar pattern. The interaction remained robust after covariate adjustment and was also observed in the joint rest-task analysis, with no significant group difference at rest. Conclusions Rapidly changing video information was associated with brain-state reorganization in youth. Douyin use was associated with lower State 7 occupancy during relatively continuous narrative segments; no significant group difference in the matched state's occupancy was detected at rest. These findings provide new evidence linking short-video viewing experience to context-dependent brain dynamics in youth.

item.title: Resting state functional connectivity associated with maternal anxiety: preliminary evidence that infant rsFC moderates the association between behavioral inhibition and anxiety/depression.
item.description:
European child & adolescent psychiatry
Postnatal maternal anxiety shapes caregiver and infant behavior. Yet, the relationship with infant brain function remains unclear. We examine the relation of maternal anxiety with infant resting state functional connectivity (rsFC). To evaluate the clinical significance of the rsFC networks identified, exploratory analyses tested whether the rsFC associated with maternal anxiety moderates risk trajectories from infant behavioral inhibition (BI) to childhood anxiety/depression symptoms. Four-month-old infants (N = 60) underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and mothers completed the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI). Analyses included 49 infants with high-quality imaging and maternal anxiety data. In the longitudinal subsample (n = 21), BI was observed at 14 months, and anxiety/depression symptoms were assessed at 4-6 years using the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL). Using whole-brain network enrichment analyses, we identified cortical network pairs that were significantly associated with maternal anxiety. Connectivity estimates from significant network pairs were averaged and tested as moderators of infant BI and childhood anxiety/depression association. Infants exposed to higher maternal anxiety showed an altered limbic-dorsal attention network (DAN) and default mode (DMN)-DAN. In both network pairs, negative and positive node-to-node pairs were identified, indicating that some regional connections exhibited stronger coupling, while others exhibited weaker coupling. Results demonstrated that DMN-DAN rsFC moderated developmental pathways: greater BI was associated with higher early-childhood anxiety/depression among infants with stronger DMN-DAN connectivity. Maternal anxiety is related to infant brain connectivity, and these neural differences moderate BI-related risk for anxiety/depression. DMN-DAN coupling may serve as an early marker of infants at risk for anxiety/depression. Given the small longitudinal sample, the moderation finding should be considered exploratory and requires replication in a larger, independent cohort.

item.title: Endogenous suspension of phenomenal consciousness during extended cessation: Regional homogeneity analysis of multi-participant 7T fMRI of an advanced meditative endpoint.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Extended cessation (EC) is a rare advanced meditative state characterized by the voluntary absence of reportable phenomenal experience, followed by reproducible aftereffects including immense mental clarity, equanimity, and peace. EC offers an endogenous model for investigating the mechanisms of consciousness. In a small-N case study (N = 3) using ultra-high-resolution 7T functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with dense within-subject sampling, we quantified whole-brain activity and related it to chemoarchitecture and cognitive maps. EC is marked by increased activity in unimodal sensory cortices and viscerosensory brainstem nuclei, and down-regulation in transmodal regions, subcortex and brainstem. Meta-analytic cognitive decoding linked EC to perceptual clarity and attentional processes, and away from distress-related domains. Multivariate coupling to normative neurotransmitter maps revealed that EC-related connectivity changes covaried with histaminergic H3 receptors topology. These findings constrain prevailing theories of consciousness by demonstrating that loss of experience need not entail global neural suppression, and supports accounts emphasizing selective precision modulation and hierarchical decoupling. More broadly, EC demonstrates that consciousness can cease without global suppression, suggesting a potential "reset" mechanism that fosters equanimity and the potential for flourishing.

item.title: In-group neural alignment serves as a biomarker of social identity.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
In this study, we propose a perspective on neural synchronization. Beyond reflecting shared understanding between individuals, we suggest it serves as a biological marker of social homogeneity. We examined fMRI neural responses of 42 participants (21 religious, 21 secular) watching neutral and religion-relevant video narratives. While explicit measures of emotional response, agreement, and engagement showed no significant differences in within-group variance, religious participants-representing a tighter social structure-exhibited significantly higher in-group neural synchrony across all content types and brain networks. Remarkably, synchrony values predicted religious orientation with an accuracy of up to 92%. We conclude that a community's homogeneous social structure drives pervasive neural alignment, positioning neural synchrony as a potential signature of group cohesion beyond explicit behavioral measures.

item.title: Network-based virtual perturbation for modeling DBS-related network effects in obsessive-compulsive and major depressive disorders.
item.description:
Psychological medicine
BACKGROUND: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) efficacy for psychiatric disorders remains heterogeneous due to incomplete mechanistic insights and insufficient individualized treatment planning. A biologically grounded computational framework is urgently needed to simulate DBS-related differences for treatment-resistant patients. METHODS: Resting-state fMRI data from 11 patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and 11 with major depressive disorder (MDD), scanned in DBS-ON and DBS-OFF states, were used to derive functional connectivity (FC) via network deconvolution. Whole-brain dynamic modeling incorporated stimulation targets, amplitudes, and frequencies to simulate DBS effects in silico. RESULTS: The model recapitulated syndrome-specific DBS-related network patterns in exploratory analyses. OCD stimulation primarily altered frontal-subcortical connectivity, whereas MDD stimulation predominantly affected default mode network hubs (p < 0.05). Under leave-one-out cross-validation, correlations between predicted and observed clinical outcomes were r = 0.625 in OCD (p = 0.040) and r = 0.659 in MDD (p = 0.028). Applying the same FC signatures to simulated FC yielded r = 0.465 in OCD (p = 0.149) and r = 0.627 in MDD (p = 0.039). In a proof-of-concept application to a separate OCD cohort (N = 92), three individuals showed high model-predicted NAc-response profiles and predicted improvement exceeding 35%. CONCLUSIONS: This hypothesis-generating framework retrospectively models DBS-related network effects using individualized resting-state FC and virtual perturbations. Linking simulated FC states with empirical DBS-ON/OFF patterns may help characterize how baseline functional architecture shapes DBS-related network responses and inform future individualized DBS modeling.

item.title: Brain-heart decoupling in somatic depression: Desynchronization between salience network neuropsychological connectivity and heart rate variability.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Somatic depression is a distinct subtype of major depressive disorder, with a poorer response to treatment, an elevated risk of suicidal behaviour, and a worse prognosis. Interoception, the sense of internal bodily signals, is related to somatic symptoms. However, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of body brain communication remain unclear. 293 depressed patients (145 with somatic symptoms and 148 without), and 160 healthy controls underwent magnetoencephalography during a resting state. Both the intra- and inter-network neural oscillation patterns of the salience network, were computed, alongside and heart rate variability (HRV) as a measure of autonomic function. Individuals with somatic depression exhibited lower HRV, accompanied by theta hyper-connectivity within the salience network. Although higher theta connectivity was linked to increased HRV in controls, this correlation was attenuated or even reversed in patients with somatic depression. Our findings identify a specific pattern of brain-heart decoupling in somatic depression, characterized by disrupted communication between salience network theta oscillations and autonomic cardiac regulation. This provides novel neuroimaging evidence for body-brain communication deficits in a clinically important depression subtype.

item.title: Scanner acoustic noise in resting-state fMRI.
item.description:
Magnetic resonance imaging
Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) is usually acquired during rapid gradient switching that produces intense, spectrally structured sound. Scanner sound activates auditory pathways and can alter neural, vigilance, autonomic, respiratory, and movement-related states, but its sound-specific causal effect on intrinsic functional-connectivity estimates remains unresolved. Direct human comparisons are few and heterogeneous: some report stronger or more extensive network estimates under quieter acquisition, whereas others find broadly preserved topology and within-network connectivity. Near-silent Looping Star imaging can recover canonical resting-state networks with marked sound reduction, but reduced temporal signal-to-noise ratio and functional sensitivity expose a trade-off between acoustic burden and measurement performance. Most quiet-versus-standard contrasts simultaneously alter temporal sampling, gradient vibration, reconstruction, steady-state behavior, or image quality and therefore identify a total protocol effect rather than a sound-specific effect. A structured, original-scale comparison reports acoustic levels and metrics, measurement conditions, acquisition parameters, and resting-state outcomes without pooling unlike measures. Vigilance, autonomic activity, respiration, and movement are potential mediators; indiscriminate regression of these variables can remove part of the total acoustic effect. Current evidence establishes that acquisition protocols can alter rs-fMRI estimates and that scanner sound is biologically active, but it does not establish a universal, directionally uniform suppression of human resting-state connectivity by conventional echo-planar imaging. Future sound-specific attribution would require randomized within-subject manipulation, protected-ear frequency-resolved dosimetry, control of co-varying vibration and sequence properties, and synchronized state and physiological monitoring.

item.title: A reproducible pipeline for simulating individual and inter-brain neural dynamics from structural connectivity.
item.description:
Journal of neuroscience methods
BACKGROUND: Computational models can link anatomical structure to neural dynamics. However, there is no validated, reproducible pipeline that simulates individual and inter-brain EEG-like dynamics from an individual's own structural connectome. NEW METHOD: To address this, we developed a comprehensive computational pipeline that combines probabilistic tractography from Diffusion Magnetic Resonance Imaging (dMRI) with dynamical systems modeling to simulate EEG-like neural dynamics from individual connectomes. It extracts anatomical connectivity, intra-individual functional connectivity, and inter-individual (two-brain) functional coupling features. It then evaluates their group-discriminative information with random-forest classification under repeated nested cross-validation. Simulated phase-locking values are calibrated against empirical resting-state EEG. RESULTS: In a test sample of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and matched controls (16 each), simulated intra-individual synchrony added classification information beyond anatomy, raising accuracy from 71.2% (AUC 0.843) to 77.6% (AUC 0.871), in a sample where groups did not differ in mean structural connectivity. COMPARISON WITH EXISTING METHODS: Unlike current single-brain simulations, this pipeline generates and jointly simulates two individual brain models within a single system, and reports the contribution of each feature level explicitly. CONCLUSIONS: The pipeline provides a reproducible, extensible framework for deriving informative individual-level dynamic features from anatomy. The two-brain extension generates and ranks candidate inter-brain features, providing a principled way to identify between-brain measures for hypothesis-driven testing.

item.title: Exposure-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Increases Connectivity Between the Central Executive and Salience Networks in Pediatric Anxiety.
item.description:
Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
OBJECTIVE: Exposure is considered the most active element of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for pediatric anxiety. Yet many youth do not respond to CBT, and exposure is the component patients most often find difficult to tolerate. Cognitive control and its supporting neural substrates may enhance exposure efficacy by helping youth remain engaged with feared stimuli despite urges to avoid. However, little work has identified how exposure-based CBT modulates intrinsic connectivity of tripartite networks that support cognitive control (e.g., central executive [CEN], salience [SN], and default mode networks [DMN]), limiting efforts to develop strategies to improve and personalize treatment. Progress may be limited by individual variability in network connectivity in anxiety, which may obscure treatment-related effects in group-averaged analyses. This randomized clinical trial (RCT) leverages person-specific network modeling to test how exposure versus relaxation components of CBT influence resting-state connectivity of cognitive control networks in pediatric anxiety. METHOD: Youth aged 7-18 years with an anxiety disorder (N = 100) or low/no anxiety (L/NA; N = 35) completed resting-state fMRI scans at baseline. Patients were randomized to exposure-focused CBT (EF-CBT) or relaxation mentorship training (RMT). Resting-state connectivity was reassessed following treatment (or after a commensurate interval in L/NA youth) in 112 participants. Changes in within-CEN, CEN-SN, and CEN-DMN density were examined using Group Iterative Multiple Model Estimation, which yields sparse, person-specific networks capturing both shared and individual connectivity structure. RESULTS: At baseline, anxious youth exhibited lower density within-CEN and between CEN-DMN than L/NA youth. Treatment effects differed by intervention: EF-CBT selectively increased CEN-SN density, whereas RMT increased within-CEN density. CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate dissociable effects of exposure and relaxation on cognitive control network organization in pediatric anxiety. These results indicate that exposure-focused CBT is uniquely associated with increased connectivity between control and salience systems, consistent with a mechanism supporting top-down control of threat-related signals during exposure. Person-specific measures of tripartite network connectivity may inform future efforts to identify candidate neural targets for optimizing and personalizing treatment.

item.title: Loneliness as a modulator of intersubject neural alignment across social and nonsocial contexts
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Loneliness is associated with cognitive biases that diverge from normative patterns of understanding and may be reflected in altered neural responses to the world. Here, we examined how loneliness modulates neural synchrony across individuals during the processing of social and nonsocial information. Using high-resolution movie-watching fMRI data ( n = 178) from the Human Connectome Project, we applied intersubject correlation analyses to identify context-dependent neural signature of loneliness. Lonely individuals primarily showed more idiosyncratic responses in regions within the default mode network, visual association cortex, and amygdala during social contexts, and in reward-related circuitry during nonsocial contexts. This suggests less stereotyped processing of social information and reward in lonely individuals. In contrast, lonely individuals exhibited greater neural synchrony in the nucleus accumbens during social contexts and in somatomotor regions during nonsocial contexts. This potentially reflects shared experiences of social craving and engagement with a socially irrelevant physical environment. These effects were robust against demographic similarities, kinship, depression, and objective levels of social connection. Together, these findings identify loneliness as a modulator of intersubject neural alignment, which may contribute to shaping how individuals process and interpret different aspects of the world.

item.title: Brain Decoding from a Deep Neural Network of Visual Memory Reveals the Maturation Trajectory of Memory Systems across Ages 3-7
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Memories from the first four years of life are largely inaccessible by adulthood, yet these early experiences profoundly shape cognition throughout development. Understanding this phenomenon of infantile amnesia is critical for revealing the mechanisms of early memory development. Here, we developed a new content-based behavioral measure of memory that quantifies how closely children’s memory patterns resemble those of adults, which we term the memory maturation score . Using a movie-watching fMRI dataset spanning age 3 to adulthood, we trained a cross-validated model on adults’ movie-evoked brain activity to predict adult’s propensity to remember each movie snippet, estimated by ResMem, a deep neural network trained to predict visual memorability. We then applied the model to each child’s brain activity while viewing the same movie to assess their memory maturation (i.e., cross-decodability from adult patterns). Children exhibited adult-like neural patterns of memory around age 4, extending prior behavioral findings. Structural analyses showed that the volume of the left posterior hippocampus, but not age or total brain volume, significantly predicted children’s memory maturation. Memory maturation around age 4 thus likely reflects age-related neural development of hippocampal memory systems, rather than an age increase itself. Functional searchlight analyses revealed a trajectory of memory maturation: the inferior temporal gyrus reflected mature memory-related processing from age 3 onward, the left posterior hippocampus by age 5, and higher-order regions involved in social-affective processing and multimodal integration by age 7. Together, these findings suggest that hippocampal maturation between ages 3 and 5 drives the maturation of memory patterns. Significance Statement Despite decades of research establishing potential mechanisms of infantile amnesia, little is known about the maturation of neural memory representations across development, limiting progress in developmental memory research and educational applications. This study reveals a developmental trajectory of memory: children show adult-like processing in the IT area by age 3, the hippocampus by age 5, and higher-order regions by age 7, reflecting mature perceptual, memory, and multimodal and social-affective processing, respectively. The left posterior hippocampus is crucial for the maturation of adult-like memory patterns. These findings show that (i) ResMem DNN can help educators select dynamic stimuli that are memorable to children by age 4, and (ii) our cross-validated model enables assessment of memory maturation without explicit memory measures.

item.title: Naturalistic recall preserves temporal specificity despite cortical feature reorganization
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Although sensory input arrives in a largely continuous stream, recall is temporally compressed, discontinuous, and often structured as events. However, the temporal specificity of recall-related neural activity within events, and the separation and cortical organization of recalled features relative to perception, remain poorly characterized. We analyzed functional MRI data recorded during viewing and free recall of an episode of Sherlock . A data-driven alignment between viewing and recall data identified neural recapitulation of corresponding narrative events and revealed information that distinguished moments within events, particularly in the association cortex. Features ranging from low-level visual to semantic information predicted recall reinstatement. However, differences in predictive performance among feature levels became smaller during recall, and their organization along the cortical sensory-to-association gradient reversed relative to viewing. Thus, temporal specificity within events can be preserved despite substantial reorganization of feature representations across the cortex during recall.

item.title: Connectivity of Implicit Statistical Learning Networks is Associated with Language Impairment Severity in Post-Stroke Aphasia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Rehabilitation of language for individuals with post-stroke aphasia (PSA) requires relearning to use cognitive-linguistic skills, but little is known about how these individuals relearn, or how brain reorganization may support different types of learning. One type of learning critical to language acquisition is implicit-statistical learning (ISL), which supports robust, accurate performance with minimal conscious effort. ISL relies on brain subnetworks that include language areas as well as domain general regions (i.e., salience and cognitive control) with the latter considered less likely to be damaged in individuals with PSA. Using three brain subnetworks previously found to be associated with ISL, the present study used graph theory metrics to (1) compare their functional connectivity in PSA (n = 30) relative to neurologically healthy controls (n=18), and (2) examine their relationship with aphasia severity in the PSA group. Resting-state functional connectivity was weaker for the language and salience subnetworks in PSA than controls, but not for the cognitive control subnetwork. Additionally, edges within all three networks correlated with aphasia severity, particularly between regions of the right frontal cortex, such that stronger connectivity in these ISL subnetworks were associated with milder aphasia. While it is unsurprising that the damaged left-sided brain regions in the PSA group resulted in connectivity that differed from controls, these differences were also observed in the salience subnetwork. Further, the correspondence to aphasia severity was evident in all subnetworks, highlighting that domain general ISL networks may contribute to variability in language outcomes.

item.title: Cumulative sport-related concussions alter cortical responses to acute aerobic exercise in rugby players.
item.description:
The Journal of sports medicine and physical fitness
BACKGROUND: Rugby athletes sustain frequent head impacts, and cumulative sports-related concussion (SRC) exposure may alter neurophysiological function beyond overt symptoms. Acute aerobic exercise can enhance cognitive performance and modulate cortical activity, yet how acute exercise influences brain-behavior responses in collision-sport athletes and whether cumulative SRC exposure modifies these responses remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of acute aerobic exercise on neurocognitive and neurophysiological responses, and to determine whether these responses are modulated by sports-related concussion exposure in young male rugby athletes. METHODS: Nineteen male rugby athletes completed resting EEG recordings (eye-opened [EO] and eye-closed [EC]; 3 min each) and cognitive testing (Stroop, King-Devick) before and after cycling at ~75% age-predicted maximal heart rate (HR). Athletes were categorized as no history of SRC (N.=8) or multiple SRC (N.=11). Exercise-related changes in cognition and relative EEG power were analyzed using repeated-measures and mixed-model Analysis of Variance (ANOVA), with associations examined using Spearman's and partial correlations. RESULTS: Stroop scores increased, and King-Devick test completion time decreased following exercise (both P<0.001). Temporal beta and gamma power showed significant time effects (EC beta P=0.026; EC gamma P<0.001; EO gamma P=0.003; EO beta P=0.050). Occipital gamma power during EO demonstrated a significant time × group interaction (P=0.012). SRC burden was negatively associated with EO occipital gamma power change (r=-0.482, P=0.037), while EO temporal gamma change was associated with King-Devick test change after controlling for SRC exposure (r=0.494, P=0.037). CONCLUSIONS: Acute aerobic exercise was associated with improved cognition and modulation of resting-state EEG activity, while cumulative SRC exposure impaired exercise-induced cortical responsivity, particularly in EO occipital gamma responses.

item.title: A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease progression.
item.description:
Science advances
Identifying the neurobiological basis of cognitive vulnerability is essential for preventing Alzheimer's disease (AD). We derived the Alzheimer's Resilience-Vulnerability Connectome (ARC) by contrasting SuperAgers (SA), an extreme phenotype of preserved late-life memory, with AD using resting-state fMRI. ARC distinguished SA from AD in a discovery cohort (N = 290; AUC = 0.85) and replicated independently (N = 143), involving prefrontal, temporal, and insular networks and associating with brain age. Applied to cognitively unimpaired adults (discovery: N = 818; replication: N = 497), ARC-based subtyping revealed SA-like and AD-like subgroups with comparable baseline cognition but divergent longitudinal trajectories. AD-like individuals exhibited faster cognitive decline, greater amyloid-β accumulation, and higher AD conversion risk. Exploratory GWAS nominated CLYBL and FRMD6 as candidate novel loci associated with the subtype difference. These findings suggest that ARC captures a continuous connectomic dimension of cognitive aging spanning SA, cognitively typical aging, and AD, highlighting the potential of functional connectomic variation for early risk stratification in AD.

item.title: Cannabidiol and fronto-parietal EEG connectivity in autistic children.
item.description:
Cerebral cortex (New York, N.Y. : 1991)
Autistic children often show altered brain network connectivity, including circuitry implicated in social cognition. Cannabidiol (CBD) has emerged as a potential therapy for autism, but its neural mechanisms remain under-researched. Here, we analyze resting-state data collected as part of a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, to explore whether 12 weeks of oral CBD oil could modulate functional connectivity in autistic children. Twenty-nine autistic children (5 to 12 years) completed two 12-week intervention periods (CBD and placebo, randomized) separated by an 8-week washout. Before and after each period, 5 min of eyes-open resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) were obtained from a subset of 18 participants (8 female). Functional connectivity was calculated across 16 electrode-pairs in the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. Beta-band connectivity between the right frontal and right inferior-parietal electrodes increased following CBD (P = 0.001, false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected P [pFDR] = 0.022), and alpha connectivity showed an increase that did not remain following FDR correction (P = 0.036, pFDR = 0.428). No significant differences were observed following placebo for any frequency band (pFDR > 0.69). This study provides preliminary evidence that 12 weeks of cannabidiol is associated with an increase in right fronto-parietal (F4-P8) functional connectivity in autistic children, most pronounced in the beta-band. Replication in larger samples is needed to confirm generalizability and clinical relevance.

item.title: Behavioural rigidity as a transdiagnostic marker of nucleus accumbens dysfunction in dementia.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Behavioural rigidity, the tendency to persist with inflexible patterns of thoughts or actions, is increasingly recognized as a transdiagnostic symptom across psychiatric, neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. Empirical studies exploring the prevalence and underlying neural mechanisms of behavioural rigidity in dementia, however, are lacking. This cross-sectional study sought to delineate the structural and functional neural correlates of behavioural rigidity using a transdiagnostic approach looking across the frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) spectrum and Alzheimer's disease (AD). A total of 204 participants were recruited, including 110 frontotemporal dementia (FTD), 53 AD and 41 healthy older control participants. Within the FTD group, 66 cases were diagnosed with clinically probable behavioural variant FTD (bvFTD), 26 presented with semantic dementia (SD) and 18 cases had progressive non-fluent aphasia (PNFA). Behavioural rigidity was assessed using the Stereotypical and Motor Behaviour subscale of the Cambridge Behavioural Inventory-Revised. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was performed to identify grey matter regions associated with behavioural rigidity transdiagnostically, the results of which informed subsequent seed-based voxel-wise functional connectivity analyses. All imaging analyses were adjusted for relevant demographic and technical covariates. Statistical thresholds were set at voxel-level P < 0.001 (uncorrected) and cluster-level P < 0.05 (false discovery rate corrected). Our main finding was that behavioural rigidity is pervasive across dementia subtypes, ranging from most pronounced in bvFTD to milder/relatively absent in PNFA, relative to controls. Whole-brain VBM across the entire patient sample revealed a significant negative association between behavioural rigidity and grey matter intensity exclusively in the bilateral nucleus accumbens. Using the bilateral nucleus accumbens as seeds, resting-state functional connectivity analysis showed that higher levels of behavioural rigidity were associated with stronger connectivity between the left nucleus accumbens and the left supplementary motor area, paracentral lobule and precuneus. This is the first study, to our knowledge, to examine the neural substrates of behavioural rigidity across FTLD syndromes transdiagnostically using structural and functional neuroimaging approaches. Our findings reveal a gradation of rigid and repetitive behaviours, most apparent in bvFTD, which in turn reflects pathological disruption of the nucleus accumbens. Taken together, our findings highlight the need to consider repetitive and rigid behaviours as a transdiagnostic feature in neurodegenerative disorders, and one which indexes underlying nucleus accumbens pathology. More broadly, this study underscores the importance of screening for rigid and repetitive behaviours in the clinic and identifies the nucleus accumbens as a promising neural target to ameliorate these symptoms.

item.title: State-specific alterations in dynamic functional network connectivity in Wilson's disease: a resting-state fMRI study.
item.description:
Neurological research
BACKGROUND: Dynamic functional network connectivity (dFNC) may reveal time-varying brain network abnormalities in Wilson's disease (WD) that are not captured by static analyses. We aimed to characterize static and dynamic large-scale network connectivity in WD using resting-state fMRI. METHODS: This retrospective study included 32 patients with WD and 32 healthy controls. Group independent component analysis identified eight components representing seven resting-state networks. Static connectivity was assessed across the full scan, while dynamic states were identified using sliding-window correlation and k-means clustering. State-specific connectivity and temporal metrics were compared between groups, and clinical associations were explored using Spearman correlation analyses. RESULTS: No sFNC difference survived false discovery rate correction. dFNC revealed group differences in States 2 and 4. In State 2, patients with WD showed increased default mode network (DMN)-left frontoparietal network connectivity and decreased DMN-dorsal attention network (DAN) and DMN-sensorimotor network connectivity. In State 4, DMN-left frontoparietal network and DAN-visual network connectivity increased, whereas DAN-right frontoparietal network connectivity decreased. Patients with WD also had shorter MDT in State 2, which correlated positively with blood urea nitrogen levels (Spearman's r = 0.478, FDR-corrected p = 0.035). CONCLUSION: WD showed state-specific changes in dynamic brain network connectivity that were not detected by static analysis. The correlation between State 2 MDT and blood urea nitrogen may reflect a relationship between brain network dynamics and peripheral metabolic status.

item.title: Network Reorganization of Right Precuneus Subregions Following Theta-Burst Stimulation.
item.description:
Brain topography
The precuneus is a heterogeneous posteromedial hub, but whether theta-burst stimulation (TBS) modulates its subregions differentially remains unclear. Here, we examined subregion-specific effects of intermittent TBS (iTBS) and continuous TBS (cTBS) applied to the right precuneus using structural MRI, resting-state functional MRI, and spectral dynamic causal modelling in 33 healthy adults scanned at baseline, post-iTBS, and post-cTBS. Three right precuneus subregions were defined as dorsal-anterior, dorsal-posterior, and ventral. Cortical thickness differed significantly across subregions, with greater thickness in the dorsal-anterior than in the dorsal-posterior and ventral precuneus. Whole-brain static functional connectivity showed significant main effects of condition and subregion, but no condition × subregion interaction. By contrast, dynamic functional connectivity revealed a significant condition × subregion interaction in the right orbital inferior frontal gyrus. Under iTBS, the ventral precuneus showed greater dynamic connectivity variability than the dorsal-anterior subregion, whereas under cTBS both dorsal subregions showed greater variability than the ventral subregion. Spectral dynamic causal modelling further demonstrated subregion-specific modulation of effective connectivity, with the most consistent between-region effects involving pathways to the left superior temporal gyrus and additional changes in self-connections. Baseline cortical thickness did not predict stimulation-induced changes in static or dynamic connectivity. These findings indicate baseline structural heterogeneity within the right precuneus and suggest that TBS related functional network reorganization differs across connectivity measures. Subregion-specific effects were most clearly expressed in dynamic and directed connectivity rather than uniformly across all connectivity measures. The results highlight the importance of subregion informed approaches for understanding and targeting precuneus centered networks.
