item.title: Metabolic complexity in the human brain supports metastable network dynamics and declines in normative ageing
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The adaptive capacity of the brain is tied to the complexity of its neural activity. While entropy of brain signals has been used to characterise this complexity in haemodynamic and electrophysiological systems, it remains unknown whether entropy contributes to the temporal dynamics of the metabolic signals of the brain (glucodynamics) and how metabolic entropy may relate to network organisation, brain ageing and cognitive decline. Here, we combined dynamic functional PET (fPET) with 18F-fluoroedeoxyglucose and simultaneously acquired functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in 84 adults to investigate multiscale entropy (MSE) in the brain. We report that metabolic complexity measured with PET MSE represents non-linear, high-frequency complexity, whereas hemodynamic complexity reflects non-linearly constrained neurovascular phase dynamics. Greater metabolic complexity was associated with greater network metastability, particularly in unimodal and higher-order associative networks. Greater regional metabolic complexity also correlated with greater cortical thickness, cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (CMRglc) and cerebral blood flow, and was lower in older than younger adults. In contrast, global and network haemodynamic MSE was not significant associated with network dynamics. Higher global metabolic complexity was associated with better cognitive performance, and voxel-level derived MSE clusters were \associated with cognitive performance in both modalities, with varied cluster sizes and spatial locations. However, these associations were largely accounted for by age variance. We conclude that temporal complexity in cerebral glucose is associated with the dynamics of the underlying metabolic signals, enables metastable network states and declines in ageing. Entropy of metabolic brain signals offers promise as a neurobiologically grounded metric of brain ageing.

item.title: Pubertal timing is a critical dimension of adolescent brain vulnerability
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Adolescence is a period of rapid brain development, during which biological maturational timing varies substantially between individuals. This variability may drive specific developmental vulnerabilities to adverse experiences with long-term consequences, warranting early identification of at-risk individuals. We utilized ultrasonic bone age measurements to track pubertal maturity, classifying participants by adolescent biological maturity relative to chronological age (accelerated, average, decelerated). Brain hierarchy was quantified as the irreversibility of brain signals in resting state electroencephalography, providing a brain-based method to detect vulnerability patterns. The COVID-19 pandemic presented a unique opportunity to also assess alterations in brain hierarchy following external disruption. We mapped maturity-defined trajectories and rates of hierarchical organization, and their post-pandemic deviation from expected development, capturing two distinct vulnerability forms. First, early maturing adolescents showed persistent reduction in brain hierarchy. Second, those undergoing their fastest phase of development – specifically, decelerated adolescents – showed the strongest disruption in brain hierarchy following the pandemic. These findings suggest that pubertal timing is a critical dimension of individual variation in adolescent brain development and vulnerability. They also emphasize the need for objective maturity measurements to tailor support to individual pubertal timelines, particularly given the secular trend toward earlier puberty and ongoing global ecological crises.

item.title: Electroencephalographic activity patterns distinguish interdigitated default and frontoparietal networks
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The brain is comprised of distributed functional networks that operate on diverse time scales. Evidence from precision fMRI shows that canonical networks, including default (DN), frontoparietal control (FPCN), and dorsal attention (dATN), each fractionate into multiple finely interdigitated networks. However, as fMRI is blind to fast processes underlying neural communication, there remains a need to neurophysiologically characterize individual-level network fractionation. To address this need, we conducted a simultaneous EEG-fMRI study, including multiple sessions per individual, resting-state and task conditions, and carbon wire loop sensors for optimized artifact correction. Using precision network mapping, we discovered dissociable electrophysiological correlates of blood-oxygen-level-dependent activity for two networks within the boundaries of the canonical DN. One (DNa) related more positively with alpha and high-beta power, while another (DNb) related more negatively with theta and low-beta power. Univariate and machine learning analyses further revealed electrophysiological dissociations between networks within the canonical FPCN (FPCNa versus FPCNb) but not dATN. The network-specific electrophysiological activity patterns were reliable across sessions, only modestly variable between resting-state and demanding task conditions, and observable for neighboring nodes of different networks across multiple cortical zones. Our findings provide insight into rhythmic neural processes that fine-grained networks may engage to support divergent cognitive operations.

item.title: Pain, Sleep, and Affective Symptoms in Primary Dysmenorrhea: A Symptom Network and Insular Connectivity Study.
item.description:
Journal of pain research
BACKGROUND: Primary dysmenorrhea (PDM) is a prevalent gynecological pain condition frequently accompanied by sleep disturbance and affective symptoms. Although neuroimaging studies have reported altered brain function in PDM, how menstrual pain relates to its multidimensional symptom profile remains incompletely understood. METHODS: A total of 113 women with PDM and 105 healthy controls (HCs) underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging during menstruation. Clinical symptoms, including the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS), Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), and Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS), were assessed using standardized questionnaires. Symptom network analysis was performed to identify core clinical symptoms in PDM. Subsequently, seed-based resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) analyses of insular subregions were conducted. Associations between altered insular connectivity and core clinical symptoms were further examined in patients with PDM. RESULTS: Symptom network analysis identified sleep disturbance and affective symptom dimensions as central or bridging features within the clinical symptom network of PDM. Compared with HCs, patients with PDM exhibited increased rs-FC between the ventral anterior insula (vAI) and regions involved in salience and cognitive-emotional processing. Exploratory Spearman correlation analyses revealed nominal positive associations between right vAI-anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) connectivity and sleep disturbance (ρ = 0.21, uncorrected P = 0.026) and anxiety (ρ = 0.26, uncorrected P = 0.005). However, neither association survived FDR correction for multiple comparisons (adjusted P = 0.194 and 0.075, respectively). CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that altered anterior insula functional connectivity may represent a neural correlate of sleep disturbance and affective symptoms in PDM. Integrating symptom network analysis with insula-centered functional connectivity analysis offers complementary perspectives on menstrual pain and its co-occurring symptoms.

item.title: The human hippocampus supports auditory coding and multisensory integration.
item.description:
PLoS biology
The hippocampus receives convergent input from multiple sensory systems, yet in humans it has been studied almost exclusively through vision. Here we examine how the hippocampus contributes to sensory processing beyond the visual modality and to the multisensory integration of visual information with these other modalities. Participants were exposed to multiple repetitions of short naturalistic movie clips, each presented in four formats: auditory-only, visual-only, congruent audiovisual, and incongruent audiovisual (audio and video from different movies). Using high-resolution fMRI, we measured univariate activation and multivariate representations across the longitudinal axis and subfields of the human hippocampus. Whereas univariate analyses detected only visual responses across hippocampal subregions, with no activation for auditory stimuli and no benefit of congruent stimuli, multivariate analyses revealed robust representations of both auditory and visual scenes. The posterior hippocampus showed enhanced pattern similarity for congruent stimuli relative to unisensory stimuli, especially in the left hemisphere, demonstrating multisensory facilitation. The anterior hippocampus showed crossmodal decoding between auditory and visual versions of the same clip, driven by the right hemisphere, suggesting a more abstract representation. Finally, whole-brain searchlight analyses revealed parallel effects in cortical regions known to support multisensory integration. These findings advance understanding of auditory and multisensory coding in the human hippocampus, revealing specialization and lateralization along its longitudinal axis.

item.title: Limbic network hyperconnectivity, fasting appetite hormone dysregulation and impaired go/no-go performance in youths with bipolar disorder.
item.description:
BJPsych open
Background Bipolar disorder in youths is associated with metabolic dysregulation, impaired inhibitory control and limbic network connectivity changes. Aims To investigate whether limbic network connectivity is associated with appetite hormones and inhibitory control in youths with bipolar disorder. Method The current study included 68 youths with bipolar disorder and 57 age- and gender-matched controls. They completed clinical assessments, the go/no-go (GNG) task, fasting appetite hormone (leptin, adiponectin, insulin and ghrelin) tests and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Region of interest (ROI)-to-ROI functional connectivity was analysed across 17 limbic ROIs. Cluster-level inferences were derived by using threshold-free cluster enhancement with family-wise error correction (p < 0.05). Furthermore, associations with appetite hormones and GNG task parameters were investigated. Results Compared with the control individuals, youths with bipolar disorder exhibited elevated leptin (p = 0.005) and insulin levels (p < 0.001), poorer performance on the GNG task and hyperconnectivity within the limbic network, identifying a significant cluster comprising the right anterior parahippocampal gyrus (aPHG)-right thalamus and right aPHG-hypothalamus edges (cluster-level family-wise error-corrected p = 0.045). No significant correlations were observed between limbic hyperconnectivity, appetite hormone levels and GNG task performance. Conclusions Current cross-sectional cohort indicates that youths with bipolar disorder exhibit concurrent alterations in appetite hormones, inhibitory control and limbic connectivity. These findings provide a characterisation of youth bipolar disorder across multiple indices, although longitudinal studies are necessary to understand how these features relate to long-term clinical trajectories.

item.title: Auditory evoked responses during ambulatory OP-MEG.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
The latest generation of optically pumped magnetometer (OPM)-based magnetoencephalography (OP-MEG) systems are increasingly portable and lightweight, making the system easier to wear while undertaking large, whole-body translational and rotational movements. We recorded OP-MEG from three participants during auditory stimulation, while the participants walked around a magnetically shielded room, moving across an area of at least 1.7 m2 and rotating by at least 180 degrees. All sensor-specific electronics were housed within a wearable backpack, minimising movement restrictions which would otherwise be imposed by sensor cabling. In this experiment, the maximum peak-to-peak range of the observed magnetic field recorded on a single channel was 25.2 nT, considerably beyond the approximately 4 nT range of many previous OP-MEG systems. We show that adaptive multipole modelling (AMM) with the temporal extension can be used to separate the interference and neuromagnetic signals, despite the large degree of movement and proximity of the sensor electronics. We observed significant auditory evoked responses at the sensor level, without the need for source localisation approaches for interference suppression. These findings demonstrate the capability of OP-MEG for conducting naturalistic experiments involving movement and for recordings with paediatric and clinical cohorts who cannot remain still.

item.title: Brain network functional connectivity alterations associated with acute posttraumatic headache.
item.description:
Headache
Objectives/background To investigate disruptions in resting state networks in participants with acute posttraumatic headache (PTH) due to mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Neuroimaging studies have demonstrated alterations in functional connectivity (FC) within core resting-state networks in participants with headache versus healthy controls (HCs), which may provide insights into disease mechanisms; however, the extent to which these alterations relate to PTH remains incompletely understood. Methods In this comparative cross-sectional study with an embedded prospective cohort, participants with acute PTH and HCs were enrolled from the Mayo Clinic Arizona and Minnesota, and the Phoenix Veterans Affairs Health Care between 2020 and 2024. Participants with PTH underwent resting-state magnetic resonance imaging within 2 months following mTBI. We investigated differences within and between functional brain networks in participants with PTH compared to HCs. Associations between altered FC with headache frequency, alterations of mood, post-mTBI symptoms, and concussion history were determined and corrected for age and sex. Relationships between PTH outcomes at 3 months and baseline FC were investigated. Results Ninety-six participants with acute PTH (35 male, 61 female) and 84 age-balanced HCs were included. Decreased resting state network connectivity in participants with PTH compared to HCs (False Discovery Rate (FDR) corrected <0.05) was observed in two default mode network (DMN) regions encompassing the bilateral frontal and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), as well as the left postcentral gyrus. Within those DMN regions, exploratory analyses revealed that FC was positively associated with headache frequency in the bilateral ACC, right precuneus and frontal gyrus, and with trait anxiety in the right ACC. In contrast, negative associations were observed between FC and number of mTBIs, as well as state anxiety, in the left ACC (uncorrected, p<0.05). No significant associations with clinical headache variables were observed in the DMN comprising the left postcentral gyrus. Baseline group differences in network connectivity between recovered and nonrecovered participants were found in visual, sensorimotor, default mode, executive control and salience networks. Alterations in baseline connectivity between independent components in recovered and nonrecovered participants were not statistically significant after corrections for multiple comparisons. Conclusion In participants with PTH, the DMN regions showing decreased connectivity also exhibited associations with headache frequency, state and trait anxiety, and number of lifetime mTBIs, suggesting that these changes relate to the severity and persistence of post-mTBI symptoms. The baseline differences in network connectivity between recovered and nonrecovered participants were not statistically significant after corrections for multiple comparisons, indicating that baseline network connections may not play a significant role in the recovery process.

item.title: Training Interbrain Synchrony through Dyadic Neurofeedback Modulates Empathy-for-Pain.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Dyadic neurofeedback offers a socially grounded approach for modulating neural processes that unfold between interacting individuals. While recent work demonstrates that dyadic neurofeedback can enhance inter-brain synchrony during interaction, whether its effects extend beyond the trained dyad remains unclear. Here, we examined whether dyadic neurofeedback targeting inter-brain synchrony in the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) is associated with changes in empathy-for-pain toward unfamiliar social targets. One hundred and eighty-six participants, randomly assigned to dyads, completed three neurofeedback training sessions within one week. Feedback was contingent on real-time IFG inter-brain synchrony in the neurofeedback group or on prerecorded signals in the sham-feedback control group. Empathy-for-pain was assessed before and after training. IFG inter-brain synchrony increased significantly across sessions in the neurofeedback group but not in the control group. Empathy-for-pain ratings showed different trajectories across conditions in the primary raw-data analysis, decreasing significantly in the sham-feedback group while remaining relatively stable in the neurofeedback group. A secondary analysis adjusting for a previously observed task-specific test-retest decline showed a significant increase in the neurofeedback group. Individuals with lower baseline trait empathy showed larger training-related increases in IFG inter-brain synchrony. Network analyses suggested broader changes involving IFG-IPL connectivity. Structural equation modeling further identified significant associations among training-related intra-brain synchrony, inter-brain synchrony, and empathy-for-pain change, consistent with the proposed relationship among these processes. Together, the findings indicate that dyadic neurofeedback can modulate IFG inter-brain synchrony across repeated training and may influence the trajectory of empathy-for-pain responding beyond the immediate training partner.

item.title: Directional Brain Connectivity Changes Induced by Heart Rate Variability Biofeedback: A Spectral Dynamic Causal Modeling Study.
item.description:
Applied psychophysiology and biofeedback
Heart rate variability biofeedback (HRVB) is a non-pharmacological intervention that trains individuals to breathe at their cardiovascular resonance frequency to enhance autonomic regulation. While HRVB improves cardiovascular function across clinical conditions, the directional neural pathways through which it modulates the central autonomic network (CAN) remain poorly understood. Using a publicly available open-access dataset, we conducted a secondary analysis of effective (directional) neural connectivity (EC) data from 32 healthy participants randomized to an 8-week HRVB intervention (n = 15) or a video game Control intervention (n = 17). Pre- and post-intervention resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data were analyzed using spectral dynamic causal modeling (DCM) combined with parametric empirical Bayes to examine group differences in EC changes (ΔEC). We also evaluated whether connectivity changes correlated with changes in peripheral autonomic regulation, indexed by the standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (ΔSDNN). Compared with the Control group, HRVB showed strong evidence (posterior-probability = 1) of increased ΔEC from the medial prefrontal cortex to the anterior cingulate cortex and bilateral thalamus post-treatment, along with reduced ΔEC from the right hippocampus to the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC). Furthermore, the regression coefficient linking hippocampus-to-VLPFC ΔEC with ΔSDNN was more (posterior-probability = 1) negative in the HRVB group than in Controls, indicating an intervention-dependent association between autonomic changes and effective connectivity. These findings indicate that HRVB may alter directional fronto-limbic communication within the CAN. Given the relatively small sample sizes, these findings need replication, but provide preliminary understanding about the neural circuitry through which resonance breathing may modulate central autonomic control.

item.title: Excessive censoring degrades individual-specific cortical parcellations and personalized TMS targets.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Head motion systematically biases functional connectivity (FC) estimates in resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI). A common mitigation strategy is to censor high-motion volumes and discard high-motion runs. However, overly stringent censoring risks discarding signal alongside noise, potentially degrading FC estimates. Here, we test the efficacy of various censoring strategies on individual-specific cortical parcellations and personalized transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) target selection. Using precision-fMRI datasets comprising 50 individuals, we define individualized "ground-truth" references from ≥1 hour of low-motion data per participant. We then simulate 10-minute or 20-minute rs-fMRI sessions with varying motion levels from the remaining data, yielding final samples of 22 and 19 participants, respectively. Higher motion produces parcellations and TMS targets that deviate further from the ground-truth references. However, at any given motion level, lenient censoring produces higher quality parcellations and personalized TMS targets than strict censoring. The improvement is comparable to doubling scan duration from 20 to 40 minutes under strict censoring. With personalized connectome-guided TMS, a common dilemma is whether to re-scan patients with only high-motion runs. A mixed-motion session with one low-motion run and one high-motion run may often be considered usable after discarding the high-motion run and strict censoring. We find that lenient censoring of high-motion-only sessions yields TMS targets comparable to-or even better than-those derived from strictly censored mixed-motion sessions. Therefore, within the motion range and parcellation/TMS targeting frameworks evaluated here, patients may not need to be re-scanned solely because all runs exceed strict censoring criteria.

item.title: Sleep Homeostasis Has Circaseptan and Circatrigintan Cycles Over Year-Long Timescales.
item.description:
Journal of sleep research
Sleep homeostasis, the process by which sleep pressure accumulated during wakefulness is dissipated across non-rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, can be quantified as the nightly rate of decline in slow-wave activity (SWA; 0.5-4 Hz). Disruption of this homeostatic process has been documented in a range of neurological disorders including epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease and REM sleep behaviour disorder, yet its long-term dynamics in healthy individuals remain uncharacterized. The advent of subscalp EEG (sqEEG) platforms now makes continuous, naturalistic sleep recording feasible over months, enabling longitudinal study of sleep homeostasis at an unprecedented scale. Here we report the first such characterization in 20 healthy adults recorded continuously over 12-15 months. SWA slope was predominantly negative across all subjects, confirming intact homeostatic regulation and was stable across sex and age. Continuous wavelet transform analysis revealed significant circaseptan (~7-day) and circatrigintan (~28-day) rhythmicity in the majority of subjects, independent of sex. These findings establish a normative baseline for long-term sleep homeostatic dynamics and suggest that homeostatic sleep pressure dissipation is organized across multiple timescales beyond the single night, with direct relevance for neurological conditions in which this process is disrupted.

item.title: Associations between nonfatal strangulation-related brain injury in intimate partner violence and resting-state functional connectivity.
item.description:
Neuropsychology
Objective Examine the association between nonfatal strangulation-related probable brain injury (NFS-BI), resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC), and verbal memory, among females who experienced physical intimate partner violence (IPV). Method Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging was analyzed for 110 females aged 18-60 years who experienced physical IPV. rsFC was characterized by seven graph theory metrics across three brain parcellation atlases (Power, Seitzman, and Schaefer-456 Parcellation[4S]). Responses to the Brain Injury Screening Questionnaire determined IPV-head trauma frequency, experience of probable NFS-BI, and other/additional non-IPV and IPV-related BI. Verbal memory was characterized by three measures from the California Verbal Learning Test, Third Edition: (a) Long Delay, Free Recall, (b) Trials 1-5 correct index scores, and (c) memory retention from Trials 1-5 to Long Delay, Free Recall. Results NFS-BI was significantly associated with reductions in within-default mode network (DMN) connectivity (Power: B = -0.03, p = .003; Seitzman: B = -0.03, p = .005; 4S: B = -0.02, p = .03), DMN segregation (Power: B = -0.04, p = .006; Seitzman: B = -0.04, p = .007; 4S: B = -0.03, p = .02), and global modularity (Power: B = -0.01, p = .02; Seitzman: B = -0.02, p = .008; 4S: B = -0.02, p = .007). Interactions between NFS-BI and within-DMN strength (Power: B = -150.05, p = .03; Seitzman: B = -212.11 p = .01; 4S: B = -204.52, p = .002), DMN segregation (Power: B = -106.97, p = .02; Seitzman: B = -114.54 p = .008; 4S: B = -189.88, p < .001), and modularity (Power: B = -373.80, p = .003; Seitzman: B = -367.35, p = .001; 4S: B = -312.55, p = .006) were significantly associated with memory retention. Conclusions Those who experienced probable NFS-BI demonstrated altered rsFC compared with those who did not. Interactions between DMN rsFC and NFS-BI were significantly associated with memory retention. Future work should assess individuals with NFS-BI longitudinally to understand its effects on long-term brain health. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

item.title: State-independent functional connectomic architecture captures transdiagnostic network alterations and clinical variation
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Psychiatric disorders show substantial overlap across diagnostic categories while differing markedly in clinical expression. Whether these shared abnormalities and individual differences are embedded in stable functional brain architecture rather than in state-specific connectivity remains unclear. Methods: We integrated functional connectomes across one resting-state and six task-based fMRI conditions in 377 participants from the YaleNeuroConnect cohort, including 223 healthy controls and 154 individuals with psychiatric disorders. Principal component analysis was applied to each participant's functional connectivity data across the seven states to derive a state-independent connectivity representation. Network-based statistics then identified components showing significant case-control differences. Cross-state consistency was assessed, and findings were validated in an independent UCLA cohort of 177 participants. Associations between component expression and clinical measures were further examined within the Yale psychiatric group. Results: Cross-paradigm connectivity revealed two reproducible patterns of state-independent network alteration. One pattern showed reduced connectivity among limbic, somatomotor and salience systems, whereas the other showed stronger cerebellar coupling with limbic and somatomotor systems. Both patterns showed consistent case-control differences across functional states and generalized to an independent UCLA cohort. Their clinical relevance, however, differed. Greater expression of the cerebello-cortical connectivity pattern was associated with lower positive affect, greater psychopathology and more everyday executive difficulties, whereas the reduced limbic-somatomotor-salience connectivity pattern showed no significant clinical associations. Conclusions: These findings delineate a stable reorganization of large-scale functional architecture across psychiatric disorders and suggest that broadly expressed psychiatric abnormalities and individual clinical variation may be differentially represented within the altered connectome.

item.title: Frontoparietal functional connectivity underlies top-down attention in mild cognitive impairment
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment frequently show attention problems such as reduced top-down control, the ability to ignore task-irrelevant information. It is unclear whether this reduction corresponds with decreased brain connectivity. We aimed to determine whether and how differences in functional connectivity, or the correlated activity between brain areas, explain differences in top-down control in amnestic mild cognitive impairment. We conducted a case-control study with 26 patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (58-91 years; 10 women) and 29 age-matched healthy older adults (60-79 years; 9 women). All patients and control participants underwent neuropsychological assessment to confirm diagnosis and healthy cognitive status, respectively. We used resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging at 3T to analyse functional connectivity. Top-down control was estimated with a 'theory of visual attention'-based verbal partial-report task (parameter α ; higher α indicates poorer control). We identified visual and attention-relevant functional brain networks and tested for differences between patients and controls while controlling for age and gender. Compared with healthy control participants, patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment showed lower functional connectivity in the left frontoparietal attention network and in one visual network and worse top-down control α (t(37.43) = -2.24, p = 0.031). The reduced connectivity in the frontoparietal network, but not the visual network, significantly correlated with top-down control α across all participants (ρ = -0.33, p = 0.003) and in the patient group (ρ = -0.48, p = 0.014). Moreover, connectivity in the frontoparietal network mediated the relationship between amnestic mild cognitive impairment and top-down control α. These results link lower frontoparietal connectivity to worse attentional control in patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment. Worse control reflects inefficient attentional selection and increasing distraction by irrelevant information during perceptual processing and encoding into working memory. Overall, this implicates a role for the frontoparietal network in maintaining cognitive control or, more generally, supporting cognitive functioning in older adults with emerging cognitive impairment.
